cues.txt: Motor control centers, or MCCs,
provide a method for grouping motor control
as well as associated distribution equipment.
In this video,
we'll explore the fundamental construction and essential role MCCs play in managing
and protecting electric motors and various industrial and commercial applications.
An MC is a freestanding electrical assembly comprised of one
or more vertical sections that share a common horizontal power bus.
Each vertical enclosed section typically contains several motor control
starter units or buckets, with each getting power
from a vertical bus that connects to the horizontal bus.
Each bucket in an MCC holds electrical parts
that control the power going to a motor or other equipment.
These parts are chosen based on the load like
voltage, current, frequency, and horsepower.
The main job of these components is to safely start
and stop the motor and protect it from problems like short circuits,
overloads, and phase failures, which can cause serious damage.
A motor starter unit can include different types of motor controls,
circuit protection,
power meters, surge protectors, energy management tools, and more.
Eaton MCCs may be applied on electrical systems up to 600V
at 50 or 60Hz, having available fault currents of up to 100,000 amps RMS.
DC motor control centers are available up to 250V DC,
having available fault currents up to 22,000 amps RMS.
Ongoing temperature and short circuit design test program as required by UL 845
ensures a quality product that meets the latest safety codes.
Let's go over the details regarding the actual MCC structure and construction.
The typical height of an MCC structure is 90 inches,
with nine inch horizontal wire ways at the top and bottom for wiring.
The remaining 72 inches are used for mounting control units, which can be arranged
in various configurations and sizes.
For front to back structures, the top horizontal wire way is 15 inches high
and the bottom is nine inches, providing 66 inches of usable space in the rear.
MCC enclosures come in various types,
including NEMA type 1, 2, 12, and 3R.
Type 3R enclosures can be non-walk-in or walk-in aisle.
Each structure includes a vertical wire way on the right side
that extends along the full height to accommodate wiring.
The top front horizontal wire spans the full width of each structure
and is isolated from the main horizontal bus.
The bottom horizontal wire way extends the full depth of the structure,
allowing for unrestricted conduit entry.
The bus system efficiently distributes power
throughout the MCC and provides mechanical strength during faults.
The vertical bus distributes three phase power
from the main horizontal bus into the vertical compartments.
It has a unique Z shape for added strength and smooth connection,
as well as the ability to mount buckets in the front and back side of the MCC.
The vertical bus is available in ratings of 600,
812 hundred amps and is made of tin plated copper for durability.
The vertical bus compartment
is isolated from the unit compartment by a full height barrier.
Optional labyrinth design barriers provide protection against phase to phase
insulation break down, and an automatic shutter mechanism
prevents exposure to the vertical bus during maintenance.
The main horizontal bus distributes three phase power
from the incoming line to each vertical structure.
It is mounted edge to edge for strength, and is available
in ratings from 600 to 3200 amps.
The bus is isolated from the top horizontal wire way by a metal barrier,
allowing easy access for maintenance.
For three-phase, four-wire applications,
a neutral landing pad is provided.
Optional half or fully rated neutral bus can be supplied.
A copper ground bus, rated at 300 amps, is mounted across the top of each
vertical structure is standard or can be mounted across the bottom,
when the bottom nine inches are not occupied by units or master terminal blocks.
Now that we have
covered the overall enclosure, bus system and wire ways, let's discuss
the actual buckets themselves that may be bolted in or removable,
and the components that get installed inside the buckets.
There is also a unique option for Eaton's FlashGard bucket
that adds an additional level of personnel safety.
Specifically designed bus stabs, insertion guides, handle mechanisms, wrapper,
terminal blocks, and safety interlocks are added to form
a standardized plug in unit that meets the highest safety standards.
Tin plated copper alloy self-winding stabs are mounted in a glass reinforced
plastic insulation block that totally shrouds each
stab, and ensures positive alignment of the stabs with the vertical bus.
The insulation block is also an integral part of the phase to phase isolation system.
The power wiring is welded to the stabs and is totally contained
within the unit enclosure, which means the vertical bus compartment
is completely free of wiring for safety and reliability.
For additional safety, Eaton's FlashGard buckets are equipped with a retractable
stab mechanism called RotoTract that withdraws the stab
assembly off the energized bus bars and into the bucket.
A spring loaded shutter then automatically closes off access to the bus bars,
which allows the electrical worker to connect and disconnect power
to the bucket with the unit door closed, thereby minimizing exposure to arc flash.
A visual indication is provided on the unit door,
showing the connect and disconnect positions of the RotoTract,
as well as the position of the shutters that enclose the stabs.
The bucket can be wrapped manually or remotely using a wired pendant
that is attached to a RotoTract remote operator,
allowing the operator to be outside the arc flash boundary.
Unit wrapper is equipped with a quarter turn side
wrapper latch that securely holds a unit to the compartment.
The latch can only be engaged when the stabs are fully mated
with the vertical bus.
Upon release of the latch, the unit can be partially withdrawn
such that the stabs disengage from the vertical bars.
In this position,
the latch can be reengaged to prevent the unit from being returned
to the fully stab position or from being removed from the structure.
The latch can be padlocked in this position to ensure
that the stabs remain disengaged during maintenance.
The handle mechanism is designed to provide a high mechanical leverage
so that little effort is required to operate any device.
The device has four positions on, off, tripped, and reset.
Only circuit breaker types have tripped and reset positions.
It is securely mounted to the front of the unit and mechanically
connected to the breaker or fusible switch, eliminating alignment problems.
The device panel can accommodate up to six 30 millimeter pilot devices such as
oil type push buttons, indicating lights, selector switches, and miniature meters.
Voltage detectors and absence of voltage testers are also available
to be installed on the device panel
and allows the end user to improve lockout, tag out procedures.
Molded into the panel or knockouts to help with future additions of devices.
Terminal blocks are mounted in knockouts on the vertical wire side of the bucket,
affording greater access to the unit compartment and its interior components.
The two piece terminal blocks snap locks together to ensure permanent
circuit continuity.
The incoming line section is where the line cables
enter the MCC from either the top or bottom,
and are easily terminated on the main lugs or connected to a main disconnect.
All incoming line sections comply with NEC
wiring bending requirements as adopted by UL.
The common equipment installed inside a bucket include
motor starters, soft starters, variable frequency drives or FDS,
a surge protection device or SPD, a power meter, and feeder disconnects.
A typical bucket used for motor protection and control
consists of a starter and a disconnect device of proven capability.
The disconnect device can be a high interrupting motor circuit protector or HMCP,
thermo-magnetic breaker, or fusible switch.
In a motor control center application, the starter's overload
relay protects the load or motor against overload currents.
The HMCP or fuse are used to permit the high inrush current of the motor
while starting, and protect the motor from high fault currents during operation.
A soft start can be used to limit inrush currents to larger motors.
A VFD can also limit inrush current and control the speed of the motor.
Feeder units are available with either molded motor case circuit breakers,
power circuit breakers, or fusible switches that feed a variety of different loads
with different power levels.
Molded case circuit breaker units are available as drawout up to 400 amps,
with dual mounting available up to 150 amps.
Units above 400 amps and up to 2500 amps are fixed mounted.
Power circuit breaker units are available as either fixed
mounted up to 2000 amps, or a draw out up to 3200 amps.
Fusible feeder units use a visible blade disconnect switch, and are mounted in
draw out units through 400 amps,
with 30 and 60 amp ratings available in dual mountings.
Fixed mounted switch ratings of 600 hundred and 800 amps are also available.
There are other special applications that can be installed in an MCC,
which include an automatic transfer switch or ATS,
transformers, panel boards and more.
An ATS can be installed to control main-tie
or main-tie-main operations of power circuit breakers or contactors.
Three-phase dry-type distribution transformers can be installed in an MCC up to 45 kVA.
They can be used to feed specific loads
or a panel board that is also mounted within the same MCC.
There is generally a high risk of arc flash associated with MCCs,
since they are commonly hard to de-energized and often worked on while hot.
Some special applications that add an extra level of safety to an MCC
are arc resistant construction, and the ability
for remote racking and operation with Eaton’s FlashGard guard buckets.
Eaton's Freedom Arc-Resistant MCCs are specifically designed to contain arc
blast energy, enhancing workplace safety with an additional layer of protection.
These MCCs are engineered with reinforced steel
latches and hinges to provide containment of internal faults
inside a space effective package that has a Type 2 accessibility rating,
ensuring arc resistance around the entire perimeter of the MCC.
The width of an arc resistant MCC is eight inches wider than a standard MCC
with four inches added to the left and to the right of the line up
to allow for gas to expand if an arc occurs.
The depth of the MCC is 21 inches and is front mount only.
The Freedom Arc-Resistant MCC does not need any venting or plenums to vent the gas,
allowing it to be mounted up against a wall
or a ceiling to be brought down to the top of the MCC.
Eaton’s Freedom FlashGard motor control centers are an industry
first in addressing the dangers associated with an arc flash event
by minimizing the risk of arc flash exposure.
This is done by using the row to track retractable
stab mechanism that was discussed earlier in this video.
In addition, a number of safety interlocks prevent scenarios where removal
or insertion of FlashGard bucket could compromise arc flash safety.
Eaton’s FlashGard arc resistant motor control centers combined
the arc containment features of Freedom Arc-Resistant motor control center,
and the arc mitigation features of Freedom FlashGard motor control centers
to provide the safest available option in the industry.
